Overview

Meta's third CyberSecEval release measures eight cyber risks of large language models in two groups: risks to third parties, where the model is an attacker's tool, and risks to application developers and their users, where the model is the attack surface (§1, Figure 1). Applied to Llama 3 and contemporary models, it finds that Llama 3 405B can run moderately persuasive multi-turn spear-phishing, like GPT-4 Turbo and Qwen 2 72B (§3.1); that in a study of 62 Meta volunteers it gave no statistically significant uplift to novice or expert attackers on easy Hack The Box machines over a search-engine baseline (§3.2, A.1); and that as an autonomous agent it handled reconnaissance but failed at exploitation (§3.3, A.2). On toy exploitation challenges Llama 3 405B led the compared models without a breakthrough (§3.4). On the application side, every model tested suggested insecure code (about 31% of autocomplete tests), prompt injection succeeded 20% to 40% of the time, and models sometimes complied with requests to abuse a code interpreter or help an attack (§4). Meta argues that its released guardrails, Prompt Guard, Code Shield and Llama Guard 3, reduce these application risks (§5).

Limits

  • A vendor assessing its own models. Meta evaluates Llama 3, concludes that its risks are comparable to peer models, and recommends its own guardrails.
  • The uplift study is small and internal. 62 Meta employees, two easy Hack The Box machines and one hour per stage, with times self-reported and then checked against terminal logs. The LLM stage always came second, so learning and time pressure are confounds, and only large effects could have been detected (A.1).
  • Simulated victims and an LLM judge. Spear-phishing targets were played by an LLM, and the judge was checked against four human raters on ten cases (§3.1).
  • A light autonomous setup. One agent with no advanced prompting, 100 steps per run, a Windows-only target, and a supplied list of leaked credentials that included a real password (A.2). The authors note that agent scaffolding has improved their earlier benchmark results up to twentyfold (§6).
  • Toy exploitation tests. Zero-shot prompts on small programs, which the authors say do not reflect real codebases (§3.4, Figure 1).
  • Small inconsistencies. The lead of Llama 3 405B over GPT-4 Turbo on exploitation is 23% in §1.1 and 22% in §3.4, and the autonomous study names Llama 3 70B in §3.3 but Llama 3.1 70B in A.2.
  • A 2024 snapshot. The models compared have since been superseded.

The other links are ours: LLM-driven spear-phishing (AIT-126, §3.1); an autonomous agent against a Windows host, whose exploit attempts all failed while no model completed a high-risk step (AIT-121, §3.3, A.2); insecure code suggestions (AIT-131, §4.2); and direct prompt injection (AIT-063, §4.1)
